<reason>CON anchored the debate to the motion's own justification—"long-term debris cascades"—and showed with plausible, ordinary examples (2008 US, 2019 India vs. 2007 China, 2021 Russia) that altitude and debris lifetime, not the bare fact of a kinetic test, determine whether that harm occurs. PRO's strongest moves (the "what we can still refuse" reframe against the minority-share point, the bright-line enforceability argument, the arson metaphor) were competent, but when pressed to name a lasting harm from the low tests PRO could not, and instead shifted to a "collision lottery" of months-long crossing risk. CON exposed that shift as abandoning the motion's stated harm and as a standard that would indict routine reentries and launches too. CON also answered PRO's sharp enforcement question honestly (neither rule binds Moscow/Beijing by force) and turned it into an incentive argument PRO never fully defused. PRO's self-grading objection was neutralized by CON's point that the same tracking network PRO relies on for verification can watch fragments decay. PRO's undeveloped "geometry lofts debris higher" point was its best residual route but got little support. CON's clipped closing is a minor execution cost; PRO's answer structure was proper. Overall CON made the decision cleaner: "all" is not needed for the harm named, and it deletes the responsible-testing path.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 2 [A4.1–A4.3] answering PRO's Q1: conceding transient risk but showing debris that reenters within weeks physically cannot seed a cascade, then flagging that PRO's "collision lottery" quietly swaps out the motion's harm—a point PRO's closing ("those months are how a cascade begins") failed to repair.</best_rebuttal>
